questions.q: What is a branch in Git?
options: A full copy of every file in the project
A movable label that points to a commit
A folder inside .git where backups are kept
questions.explain: A branch is just a lightweight label on a commit. That's why creating one is instant, and why it moves forward when you commit.

options: Which branch (or commit) you are on right now
The first commit in the project
questions.explain: HEAD points to the branch you have checked out. Git Bash shows it in the prompt, e.g. (feature-menu).

questions.q: Which commands create a new branch AND switch to it? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explain: switch -c and checkout -b both create and switch. git branch <name> only creates; you are still on the old branch.

questions.q: Krish added a line to menu.txt and committed it on feature-menu. What does the last command print?
questions.explain: Switching branches changes your files to match that branch. His line is safe on feature-menu, but main doesn't have it yet.

questions.q: You want feature-cart's work in main. Which is correct?
options: git switch feature-cart, then git merge main
git switch main, then git merge feature-cart
git merge main feature-cart from any branch
questions.explain: Merge INTO the branch you are on: first switch to the branch that receives the changes (main), then merge the other one in.

questions.q: When does Git do a fast-forward merge?
options: When both branches have new commits
When the branch you are on has no new commits since the other branch started
questions.explain: If main didn't move, Git just moves the main label forward to the other branch's commit. No merge commit is created.

questions.q: When does a merge conflict happen?
options: Whenever two people use the same repository
When two branches changed the same lines of the same file
When you merge more than once a day
When a file is added on one branch
questions.explain: Git merges different lines automatically. Only when both sides changed the same lines does it stop and ask you to decide.

questions.q: Put the steps to resolve a conflict in timing.txt in order.
items: Open timing.txt and choose the correct text
questions.explain: Edit the file, remove every marker, mark it resolved with git add, then commit to finish the merge.

questions.q: In this conflicted file, which line is YOUR version (the branch you are on)?
questions.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
Open: 10 AM
=======
Open: 8 AM
>>>>>>> change-timing
questions.explain: The part between <<<<<<< HEAD and ======= is your version; between ======= and >>>>>>> is the branch being merged.

questions.q: You're halfway through a messy merge and want to start again. What do you run?
questions.explain: git merge --abort puts the working tree and index back exactly as they were before the merge.

questions.q: git branch -d experiment says the branch 'is not fully merged'. What does that mean?
options: The branch has commits that are not in your current branch; deleting it would abandon them
The branch name is spelled wrong
questions.explain: -d refuses to delete unmerged work. If you are sure you don't need it, -D forces the deletion.

questions.q: Which are good team branching habits? (Choose all that apply.)
options: Pull before starting a new branch
Do all work directly on main to avoid merges
questions.explain: Working directly on main means the shared version is often broken. Small feature branches keep conflicts small.
